name: journal-was-paul-a-roman-citizen.json
content:
Was Paul a Roman citizen? Acts says so three times. Paul never says so once. A claim that appears only in the biography and never in the man's own letters needs a closer look than it usually gets.

What Acts says

At Philippi, the magistrates had Paul and Silas beaten with rods and thrown into prison.1 Only the next day does Paul play the card: "They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison."2 The magistrates "were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens".3 The claim arrived after the beating, when it was too late to prevent it.

In Jerusalem the tribune had Paul stretched out for the whips when Paul asked: "Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?"4 The tribune answered: "I bought this citizenship for a large sum." Paul said: "But I am a citizen by birth."5 Later, before the governor, Paul appeals to Caesar, which only a citizen could do.6

[paulus_figure name="roman-silver-coins"]Roman silver coins. Acts gives Paul a citizen's rights; his letters never claim them.[/paulus_figure]

What Paul says

Paul wrote seven letters this site treats as his own. In none of them does he mention Roman citizenship, a Roman name, an appeal to Rome or a protection that Roman law gave him. He tells the Philippians, in a letter to a Roman colony, that he was "circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee".7 It is a list of credentials. Citizenship of Rome, if he had it, was the most valuable credential in the empire. He leaves it out.

The only citizenship he mentions in that letter is a different one: "our citizenship is in heaven".8 The Philippians knew the value of the other kind. Their city was proud of its Roman status. A man who held it would not have missed the chance to say so.

The rods

Paul does record being beaten. "Three times I was beaten with rods."9 Roman law protected citizens from this treatment. Cicero, prosecuting the governor Verres, said that it is a crime to bind a Roman citizen and a wickedness to scourge him.10 A citizen who was beaten three times had either failed to say so or been ignored.

Acts records one rod beating, at Philippi, and has Paul speak up only after the fact. The letters record three. If Paul was a citizen, he suffered the penalty the law forbade and said nothing to anyone each time. If he was not, then Acts has given him a status that his own account of his suffering contradicts.

A citizen of Tarsus?

Acts also gives Paul a hometown. "I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city."11 Paul's letters never name Tarsus. He says he went "into the regions of Syria and Cilicia" after Damascus, and he places himself in the tribe of Benjamin, not in a Greek city.12 Acts also says that Saul "was also called Paul", a Roman name, but a name proves little. Provincials took Roman names without holding Roman citizenship, and the letters do not claim the rights that went with one.

A story for Roman readers

Acts is written to be read by people who could hurt the church, and it keeps showing Roman officials treating Paul with respect. Gallio, the governor of Achaia, dismisses the charges against him: "I refuse to be a judge of these things."13 Festus and Agrippa confer and agree: "This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment."14 The citizenship is the thread that ties these scenes together. It gives Rome a reason to protect him and gives Luke a way to show that the movement was no threat to the empire.

What the claim does for Luke

The claim has one more use. It turns Paul's arrest into a trial before Roman officials, and it carries him by Roman ship to Rome, where Acts ends. Without citizenship, Luke has no way to get his hero to the capital under official escort, no courteous tribune and no hearing before Festus and Agrippa. The device explains how Paul gets from Jerusalem to the empire's centre. [paulus_link slug="the-citizenship-and-the-appeal-to-caesar" /] sets out each use in turn, and [paulus_link slug="paul-in-prison" /] follows the chains to the end of Acts.

The verdict

The Roman citizenship of Paul rests on Luke alone. Paul wrote seven letters, listed his credentials to a Roman colony and recorded being beaten with rods three times, and he never claims a status that would have made every one of those beatings illegal.

The simplest explanation is that Luke gave him the citizenship because the story needed it. [paulus_link slug="tarsus-and-a-persona-for-every-audience" /] follows the same habit through the other credentials Acts hands Paul.

Paul and Roman citizenship: questions readers ask

Was Paul a Roman citizen?

Acts says so at Philippi, in Jerusalem and in his appeal to Caesar. None of his letters mentions it.

How did Paul become a citizen?

Acts says he was one by birth (Acts 22:28) and gives no account of how his family obtained it.

Was Paul beaten with rods?

By his own account, three times (2 Corinthians 11:25). Acts records one beating with rods, at Philippi.

Did Paul appeal to Caesar?

Acts says so (Acts 25:11). No letter mentions an appeal to Caesar.
